indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics
indicator.description: A market-wide daily snapshot from CoinMarketCap containing aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, trading volume, market-share measures, sector-level market capitalization and volume, derivatives activity, market growth rates, and ecosystem activity statistics. The dataset provides a broad view of crypto-market size, liquidity, market structure, capital distribution, and changes in market activity within a single observation.
indicator.use: Monitor the overall size, liquidity, composition, activity, and structural changes of the cryptocurrency market using CoinMarketCap's aggregate market metrics.
indicator.purpose: Provide a consolidated market-wide snapshot for understanding total crypto-market capitalization, trading activity, Bitcoin and Ethereum market share, altcoin and DeFi market size, stablecoin liquidity, derivatives activity, and changes in the broader crypto ecosystem.
indicator.significance: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics provides broad market context that can be used to interpret changes across individual crypto assets and specialized indicators. Total market capitalization measures the aggregate value of the cryptocurrency market, while 24-hour spot trading volume provides a measure of market activity and liquidity. Altcoin market capitalization and volume help isolate activity outside Bitcoin, while Bitcoin and Ethereum dominance measure their respective shares of the total cryptocurrency market and can provide context for capital distribution and rotation. DeFi market capitalization and volume provide visibility into decentralized-finance activity, while stablecoin market capitalization and volume provide context for the size and activity of crypto-native liquidity instruments. Derivatives volume provides a measure of activity in crypto derivatives markets. The dataset also includes daily percentage changes in total market capitalization, total volume, DeFi activity, stablecoin activity, and derivatives activity, allowing the system to identify rapid changes in market conditions. Active cryptocurrency, market-pair, and exchange counts provide additional context for the size and breadth of the crypto ecosystem. These metrics can be analyzed alongside asset prices, market breadth, volatility, derivatives positioning, funding rates, stablecoin indicators, Bitcoin dominance, DeFi indicators, and macroeconomic conditions to identify changes in liquidity, market participation, capital rotation, and broader crypto-market regimes.

indicator.name: Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index from Alternative.me measuring crypto-market sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, where lower values represent greater fear and higher values represent greater greed. Alternative.me derives the index from multiple sentiment-related inputs, including Bitcoin volatility, market momentum and volume, social media activity, surveys, Bitcoin dominance, and Google Trends. Alternative.me's published methodology currently identifies the index as Bitcoin-focused.
indicator.use: Track daily changes in aggregate crypto-market sentiment using Alternative.me's composite Fear & Greed Index and its fear-to-greed classification.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized daily measure of market sentiment that can be used to identify shifts between fear, neutrality, and greed in the crypto market.
indicator.significance: The Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index combines multiple market and sentiment signals into a single 0-to-100 measure. Alternative.me's published methodology assigns 25% weight to volatility, 25% to market momentum and volume, 15% to social media, 15% to surveys, 10% to Bitcoin dominance, and 10% to Google Trends, although Alternative.me currently states that its surveys are paused. The index therefore captures several dimensions of market behavior rather than directly measuring investor sentiment through a single survey. It can be analyzed alongside price trends, volatility, trading volume, derivatives positioning, funding rates, market breadth, Bitcoin dominance, and other sentiment indicators to provide broader context for changes in crypto-market conditions.

indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index
indicator.description: A daily CoinMarketCap index measuring the relative performance of major altcoins versus Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period. The index uses the top 100 eligible coins ranked on CoinMarketCap, excluding stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens, and scales the proportion of coins outperforming Bitcoin to a 0-to-100 index.
indicator.use: Track the degree to which major altcoins are outperforming or underperforming Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period and identify shifts between Bitcoin-dominant and altcoin-dominant market regimes.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized measure of altcoin market breadth relative to Bitcoin and identify broad changes in relative performance across the cryptocurrency market.
indicator.significance: The CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index measures market breadth by comparing the rolling 90-day performance of the top 100 eligible coins on CoinMarketCap against Bitcoin. Stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens are excluded from the constituent set. The index reflects the proportion of these coins outperforming Bitcoin and is scaled from 1 to 100. Values above 75 indicate Altcoin Season, while values at or below 25 indicate Bitcoin Season. The index therefore measures the breadth of altcoin outperformance rather than sentiment directly: a high value means a large share of major altcoins have outperformed Bitcoin over the measurement period, while a low value means relatively few have done so. It can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin dominance, altcoin market capitalization, market breadth, liquidity, trading volume, and crypto-market sentiment to provide context for changes in market regime and capital rotation.

indicator.name: Bitcoin Spot ETF Market
indicator.description: A daily measure of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market activity, including aggregate net capital flows, traded value, net assets, and cumulative net flows. The indicator provides a view of capital entering or leaving the Bitcoin spot ETF market and the size and activity of the investment vehicles providing regulated market access to Bitcoin.
indicator.use: Track daily capital flows, trading activity, assets under management, and cumulative capital flows in the U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a daily view of institutional and traditional-finance market participation in Bitcoin through regulated spot ETF vehicles and identify changes in capital allocation toward Bitcoin.
indicator.significance: Bitcoin spot ETF market data provides a direct view of capital flows and asset levels within regulated investment vehicles that give traditional investors access to Bitcoin. Net flow measures the daily net movement of capital into or out of the ETF market, while value traded measures ETF trading activity. Net assets indicate the aggregate size of assets held through the ETF vehicles, and cumulative net flow tracks the longer-term accumulation of capital flows since the measurement period began. Bitcoin ETF activity can provide important context for institutional and traditional-finance participation in Bitcoin and can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin price, Bitcoin dominance, derivatives positioning, open interest, funding rates, macroeconomic conditions, inflation expectations, interest rates, Treasury yields, liquidity conditions, and broader crypto-market sentiment. ETF flows should be interpreted as activity within the spot Bitcoin ETF market and should not be treated as a complete measure of all institutional Bitcoin ownership or total Bitcoin demand.

indicator.use: Track changes in Bitcoin futures open interest and positioning across dealers, asset managers, leveraged funds, other reportable traders, and nonreportable traders, including shifts in long, short, spreading, and net exposure.
indicator.purpose: Provide asset-specific visibility into how different classes of market participants are positioned in Bitcoin futures and how their exposure changes over time.

Changes in open interest reveal changes in futures-market participation, while changes in long and short positions show how each trader group is adjusting directional exposure. Separating trader classifications allows the intelligence system to distinguish institutional and leveraged positioning from dealer activity and aggregate nonreportable participation when analyzing Bitcoin market structure and sentiment.

indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the two-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing interest-rate expectations, monetary policy, financial conditions, and relationships across the yield curve.

indicator.name: 10-Year Treasury Yield

indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the ten-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing long-term interest rates, economic expectations, monetary policy transmission, and financial market conditions.
indicator.significance: The 10-year Treasury yield is a major benchmark for U.S. long-term interest rates and influences pricing across financial markets. Changes in the yield can reflect shifts in expectations for inflation, economic growth, monetary policy, and demand for government securities.

indicator.name: Real 10-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury securities whose principal and interest payments are adjusted for inflation. It represents a market-based measure of the real interest rate for a 10-year maturity.
indicator.use: Monitor real long-term interest rates and assess changes in inflation-adjusted borrowing costs, financial conditions, and market expectations.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the real 10-year U.S. interest rate for analyzing real borrowing costs, inflation-adjusted returns, monetary policy, and financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The real 10-year Treasury yield provides information about the inflation-adjusted cost of long-term capital and the pricing of inflation-indexed government securities. Changes in the yield can affect financial conditions and the relative attractiveness of real versus nominal assets.

indicator.name: M2 Money Supply
indicator.description: A broad measure of the U.S. money supply consisting of currency and deposits and other liquid assets included in the Federal Reserve's M2 monetary aggregate. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the quantity of money circulating through the U.S. financial system and assess changes in liquidity and monetary conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of the U.S. money supply for analyzing monetary conditions, liquidity, financial activity, and relationships between money growth and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: M2 provides a broad measure of money and liquid deposits available within the U.S. financial system. Changes in M2 can provide information about shifts in monetary and liquidity conditions and can be analyzed alongside inflation, interest rates, credit, and economic activity.

indicator.name: Reverse Repo Usage
indicator.description: The aggregated daily amount of overnight reverse repurchase agreement transactions conducted by the Federal Reserve with eligible counterparties. The series is not seasonally adjusted and is reported in billions of U.S. dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor usage of the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility and assess changes in short-term liquidity and money-market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of overnight reverse repo activity for analyzing Federal Reserve open-market operations, money-market liquidity, reserve conditions, and changes in short-term financial conditions.
indicator.significance: Reverse repo usage reflects the amount of funds placed into the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility by eligible counterparties. Changes in usage can provide information about money-market conditions, the distribution of liquidity, and the interaction between Federal Reserve operations and short-term interest rates.

indicator.name: Nominal Broad U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the value of the U.S. dollar against a broad group of foreign currencies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the broad nominal value of the U.S. dollar and assess foreign-exchange conditions, international financial conditions, trade competitiveness, and cross-border capital flows.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. dollar strength against major trading-partner currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, monetary policy transmission, global financial conditions, and relationships between the dollar and other asset markets.
indicator.significance: The broad U.S. dollar index provides a trade-weighted measure of changes in the dollar's value across a broad set of foreign currencies. Changes in the index can affect import prices, export competitiveness, international capital flows, commodity pricing, and global financial conditions.

indicator.name: Nominal Advanced Foreign Economies U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the nominal value of the U.S. dollar against currencies of advanced foreign economies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the U.S. dollar's nominal value against currencies of advanced foreign economies and assess exchange-rate conditions, international financial conditions, and cross-border economic relationships.
indicator.purpose: Provide a trade-weighted measure of the U.S. dollar against advanced-economy currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, relative currency movements, monetary policy transmission, and international financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The index isolates movements in the U.S. dollar relative to currencies of advanced foreign economies using trade-weighted exchange rates. Changes can provide information about dollar strength, international capital conditions, trade relationships, and differences in monetary and economic conditions across major advanced economies.

indicator.name: Consumer Price Index
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted price index measuring changes in the prices paid by urban consumers for a broad basket of goods and services in the United States. The index is based on a reference period of 1982–1984 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in consumer prices and assess inflation and deflation across the broad basket of goods and services purchased by urban consumers.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of changes in consumer prices for analyzing inflation trends, purchasing power, monetary policy, and economic conditions.
indicator.significance: The CPI is one of the primary measures used to monitor consumer price changes in the U.S. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in inflationary or deflationary conditions and are relevant to monetary policy, household purchasing power, and economic analysis.

indicator.name: Personal Consumption Expenditures
indicator.description: A measure of spending by households on goods and services in the United States. The series is reported as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor household consumption and changes in consumer spending, a major component of U.S. economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of personal consumption expenditures for analyzing consumer demand, economic growth, household spending behavior, and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: Personal consumption expenditures represent a major component of U.S. economic activity. Changes in consumer spending can provide information about household demand, economic momentum, and shifts in consumption patterns.

indicator.name: Nonfarm Payrolls

indicator.use: Monitor changes in total nonfarm employment and assess labor-market conditions, job creation, and changes in overall economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. employment for analyzing labor-market strength, economic growth, household income, business activity, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: Nonfarm payrolls are a major measure of U.S. employment and provide information about changes in the number of jobs across the economy. Sustained increases or decreases can provide insight into labor-market conditions and broader economic momentum.

indicator.name: Unemployment Rate

indicator.use: Monitor labor market conditions and changes in the share of the labor force that is unemployed.
indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of U.S. labor market conditions for analyzing employment, economic activity, monetary policy, household conditions, and changes in the business cycle.

indicator.name: CNN Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index designed by CNN to measure prevailing fear and greed in the U.S. stock market using multiple market-behavior indicators. The index ranges from 0 to 100, with lower values representing greater fear and higher values representing greater greed.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in U.S. equity-market sentiment, investor risk appetite, market momentum, volatility, and demand for defensive assets, and identify shifts between risk-seeking and risk-averse market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a compact market-sentiment signal that summarizes several observable characteristics of U.S. equity markets into a single daily measure for tracking changes in investor risk appetite and market stress.
indicator.significance: The Fear & Greed Index provides a behavioral measure of the prevailing emotional conditions in U.S. equity markets. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in market momentum, volatility, demand for safe-haven assets, and willingness to take risk. It can therefore provide context for interpreting market moves alongside prices, volatility measures, credit conditions, and broader financial-market indicators.

indicator.name: CNN Market Volatility (VIX vs 50-Day Moving Average)
indicator.description: A daily market-volatility indicator based on the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) relative to its 50-day moving average. The VIX reflects expected S&P 500 volatility over the following 30 days, while its relationship with the 50-day average is used by CNN as a measure of changing market volatility and fear.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in expected U.S. equity-market volatility and identify shifts in market stress, risk aversion, and investor sentiment through the VIX's relationship with its 50-day trend.
indicator.purpose: Provide a volatility-based measure of U.S. equity-market conditions that captures whether expected market volatility is increasing or decreasing relative to its recent trend.
indicator.significance: The VIX provides a forward-looking measure of expected S&P 500 volatility derived from options prices. Comparing it with its 50-day moving average adds a trend dimension that helps identify changes in market stress and risk perception. Rising volatility relative to its trend is interpreted by CNN as a signal of fear, while declining volatility is associated with greed. As one component of the Fear & Greed framework, it complements momentum, breadth, options positioning, and other measures of market behavior.

indicator.name: CNN Safe Haven Demand
indicator.description: A daily measure of the difference between U.S. Treasury bond and stock returns over the previous 20 trading days. It is used by CNN to assess whether investors are favoring safer Treasury assets over riskier equities.
indicator.use: Monitor shifts between equity risk-taking and demand for safer Treasury assets, and identify changes in investor risk appetite, defensive positioning, and market stress.
indicator.purpose: Provide a cross-asset measure of investor risk preference by comparing recent stock and Treasury performance over a 20-trading-day period.
indicator.significance: Safe Haven Demand captures changes in investor preference between riskier equities and safer Treasury assets. When Treasury bonds outperform stocks, it can indicate increased demand for defensive assets and greater risk aversion; when stocks outperform Treasuries, it indicates stronger relative demand for risk assets. As a component of CNN's Fear & Greed framework, it adds a cross-asset risk-preference signal that complements equity momentum, breadth, volatility, and options positioning.

indicator.name: AAII Investor Sentiment Survey
indicator.description: A weekly survey of individual investors measuring the percentage who expect the U.S. stock market to rise, remain essentially unchanged, or fall over the next six months. The dataset includes bullish, neutral, bearish, and bull-bear spread readings.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in individual-investor expectations, optimism, pessimism, uncertainty, and overall sentiment toward the U.S. stock market, including changes in the bull-bear spread.
indicator.purpose: Provide a direct survey-based measure of individual-investor expectations that complements market-derived sentiment indicators by capturing what retail investors expect the stock market to do over the following six months.
indicator.significance: The AAII Sentiment Survey provides a direct measure of individual-investor expectations rather than inferring sentiment from market prices or positioning. Changes in bullish, neutral, and bearish responses reveal shifts in optimism, pessimism, and uncertainty, while the bull-bear spread summarizes the balance between optimistic and pessimistic views. Extreme sentiment readings can provide useful context for assessing investor psychology and potential sentiment reversals, but the survey does not establish the future direction of the market.

indicator.name: IG Gold Retail Positioning
indicator.description: A daily measure of long and short positioning among retail traders on the IG trading platform for gold. The indicator reports the percentage of IG retail traders holding long and short positions and the resulting net positioning. This data represents IG's own retail trader pool and is not a market-wide measure of all retail traders or investors.
indicator.use: Track daily changes in long and short positioning among IG retail traders exposed to gold, including the distribution of positions and the resulting net retail positioning.
indicator.purpose: Provide a daily view of how IG's retail trader population is positioned toward gold and how that positioning changes over time.
indicator.significance: IG gold retail positioning provides a daily view of directional exposure among retail traders using the IG trading platform. The indicator can provide context for retail sentiment, speculative positioning, and changes in exposure to gold. Because the dataset represents only IG's retail trader pool rather than the entire retail-investor population, it should be interpreted as a broker-specific positioning signal rather than a comprehensive measure of overall retail sentiment. Gold positioning can be analyzed alongside gold prices, safe-haven demand, inflation expectations, real interest rates, Treasury yields, the U.S. dollar, Federal Reserve policy, and broader financial-market conditions to provide additional context for changes in gold-market positioning.

results.title: Thailand Clears Path for Bitcoin, Ether ETFs on Stock Exchange
highlights: Thailand Clears Path for Bitcoin, Ether ETFs on Stock Exchange Thailand finalizes rules paving way for Bitcoin, Ether ETFs Latest News Published Oct 9, 2026 The rules are set to take effect next week, allowing crypto ETFs to trade exclusively on the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Update ( Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday finalized rules allowing crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to list on Thailand’s main stock exchange, limited initially to Bitcoin and Ether. The regulator said the rules will take effect on Oct. 16, 2026. Crypto ETFs must be listed for trading exclusively on the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Products linked to foreign crypto ETFs, such as depositary receipts, will not be permitted initially, while Thai brokers will remain barred from facilitating investments in overseas crypto ETFs for retail investors outside institutions and ultra-high-net-worth individuals. The framework opens a new route for Thai investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin and Ether through the stock market. The SEC also amended its rules to allow mutual funds and private funds to invest in Thai-established crypto ETFs, whereas previously they could invest only in foreign crypto ETFs. Issuers still need to complete fund registration, obtain product approval, secure a SET listing and arrange custody before launching, Fuwattananukul said. The framework also prohibits brokers from providing margin loans to purchase crypto ETFs and requires fund assets to be held with SEC-regulated digital asset custodians. Investors must receive information about the products and confirm that they understand the risks before trading. Crypto ETFs must be managed as a passive investment vehicle seeking to track the price of the crypto asset in which it invests. It must maintain net exposure to a single cryptocurrency averaging at least 80% of net asset value over each accounting year. The SEC consulted on the proposed principles in April and May and on draft regulations in August and September. Most respondents supported the proposals, the regulator said.

results.title: Thailand SEC issues bitcoin and ether ETF rules set to take effect Oct. 16
highlights: Thailand SEC issues bitcoin and ether ETF rules set to take effect Oct. 16 Thailand SEC issues bitcoin and ether ETF rules set to take effect Oct. 16 The Thai regulator set an Oct. 16 effective date for its crypto ETF framework, while limiting initial assets to bitcoin and ether. - Initial funds will be limited to bitcoin and ether, must maintain average exposure of at least 80% to a single crypto asset, and use SEC-regulated custodians. Thailand will initially allow only bitcoin (BTC) and ether (ETH) in cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds under rules issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the regulator said in a statement on Thursday. Slated to take effect on Oct. 16, the rules require funds to track crypto asset prices and maintain average net exposure of at least 80% of net asset value to that asset over each accounting year. The funds must also use custodians licensed by the SEC and trade exclusively on the Stock Exchange of Thailand, according to the statement. The SEC said investors will have to acknowledge the risks of crypto ETFs before trading, while securities firms will be barred from offering margin loans to finance purchases. On asset managers, the securities watchdog said they can outsource their services only to licensed digital asset fund managers. Meanwhile, qualified digital asset firms can supervise crypto ETFs, provided they meet requirements for financial standing, staffing, and operational systems, the regulator said. The SEC said Thai mutual funds and private funds will be allowed to buy locally listed crypto ETFs under the rules. Previously, they could invest only in foreign crypto ETFs, although existing investment limits still apply. However, the regulator also prohibited the issuance and offering of depositary receipts linked to foreign crypto ETFs during the initial phase. Securities firms cannot arrange foreign crypto ETF investments for clients outside the institutional and ultra-high-net-worth categories, per the statement.

results.title: Crypto ETF News Today: ETFs Outflows After Fed Minutes
highlights: Crypto ETF News Today: BTC, ETH, SOL Outflow After Fed Minutes Meeting Deepmala Upadhyay Published: October 8, 2026 Last Updated: 08 Oct 2026 Red candles greeted investors across every major crypto ETF today. If you checked your portfolio this morning, you already know why this is the Crypto ETF news today story everyone is talking about. Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP funds all felt the squeeze, and the Federal Reserve's own words played a big part in it. - Bitcoin ETFs posted their biggest outflow of October, with -$487.07M leaving on October 7, the largest since June 25, 2026. - Ethereum ETFs lost -$160.77M, Solana ETFs saw a third straight outflow day, and XRP ETFs recorded zero flow for the second time this month. - The September Fed meeting minutes, where all 19 officials backed a rate hike, fed into a wider crypto market crash that hit BTC, ETH, XRP and SOL prices alike. This crypto market crash did not happen on its own. The Fed meeting minutes release from the September meeting is the main trigger behind today's selloff and ETF outflows. As per The Kobeissi Letter, most Fed officials now expect another interest rate hike before the year ends. All 19 Fed officials backed the September hike. Nearly everyone on the committee sees inflation risks pointing upward, and some officials even warned that AI-driven demand could outpace supply and push prices higher. Higher rate expectations push investors away from risk assets like crypto, and that is exactly what today's ETF outflows show. Bitcoin ETF outflow numbers tell the clearest story today. As per SoSoValue data, Bitcoin spot ETFs saw a daily net outflow of -487.07million on October 7. That makes it the biggest outflow of October, and the largest since June 25, 2026, when outflows hit -696.29 million. Out of 12 ETF providers, 7 recorded outflows today. BlackRock led the exit with $207.67 million pulled out, followed by Fidelity at $105.15 million and Ark & 21Shares at $101.71 million. Ethereum ETF outflow followed a similar pattern. Daily net outflow came in at -$160.77 million, the second largest outflow of October. Out of 11 providers, 7 recorded outflows today. BlackRock led again with $116.05 million pulled out, Grayscale's ETHE fund lost $25.77 million, and 21Shares saw $6.27 million leave. XRP news took a different turn today. Daily net flow was exactly $0.00, the second time this month that XRP ETFs have gone silent. That follows the biggest inflow of the month, $4.07 million on October 1, and an outflow of $3.28 million on October 2. Solana outflow data shows a short but steady slide. Today's daily net outflow was -$4.80 million, the third consecutive day of outflows this month. Bitwise led the exit, accounting for the entire $4.80 million pulled out. Not everything in this story is bearish. Analyst Nate Geraci pointed out that the SEC has approved listing and trading of the first 3x leveraged Bitcoin and Ether ETFs. That is a big shift when you remember that less than three years ago, the SEC had not even concluded its lawsuit against Grayscale over a plain spot Bitcoin funds. Additionally, Pepe and SEI ETFs could be on the way next, though these remain filings to watch than approved products. Expert Opinion: Market analysts note that outflows after a hawkish Fed signal are a familiar pattern rather than a new phenomenon. results.title: 2026 Digital Asset Outlook: Dawn of the Institutional Era
highlights: - We expect 2026 to accelerate structural shifts in digital asset investing, which have been underpinned by two major themes: macro demand for alternative stores of value and improved regulatory clarity.Together, these trends should bring in new capital, broaden adoption (especially among advised wealth and institutional investors), and bridge public blockchains more fully into mainstream financial infrastructure. - Grayscale expects bipartisan crypto market structure legislation to become U.S. law in 2026. This will bring deeper integration between public blockchains and traditional finance, facilitate regulated trading of digital asset securities, and potentially allow for on-chain issuance by both startups and mature firms. - We expect more crypto assets to be available through exchange-traded products in 2026. These vehicles have had a successful start, but many platforms are still conducting due diligence and working to incorporate crypto into their asset-allocation process. As this process matures, look for more slow-moving institutional capital to arrive throughout 2026. Second, regulatory clarity is driving institutional investment into public blockchain technology. It can be easy to forget, but until this year the U.S. government had outstanding investigations and/or lawsuits with many leading firms in the crypto industry, including Coinbase, Ripple, Binance, Robinhood, Consensys, Uniswap, and OpenSea. Even today, exchanges and other crypto intermediaries operate without clear spot-market guidelines. This ship has slowly been turning. In 2023, Grayscale won its lawsuit against the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission), which paved the way for spot crypto exchange-traded products (ETPs). In 2024, Bitcoin and Ether spot ETPs came to market. In 2025, Congress passed the GENIUS Act on stablecoins and regulators shifted their approach toward crypto, working with the industry to provide clear guidance while continuing to focus on consumer protection and financial stability. In 2026, Grayscale expects Congress to pass bipartisan crypto market structure legislation, which will likely cement blockchain-based finance in U.S. capital markets and facilitate continued institutional investment (Exhibit 4). New capital entering the crypto ecosystem is likely to come primarily through spot ETPs, in our view. Since the Bitcoin ETPs launched in the U.S. in January 2024, global crypto ETPs have seen net inflows of $87 billion (Exhibit 5). Despite the early success of these products, the process of incorporating crypto into mainstream portfolios is still in early innings. Grayscale estimates that less than 0.5% of U.S. advised wealth is allocated to the crypto asset class.[2] This number should grow as more platforms complete their due diligence, build out capital market assumptions, and incorporate crypto into model portfolios. Beyond advised wealth, early movers have already adopted crypto ETPs in institutional portfolios, including Harvard Management Company and Mubadala (one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds).[3] We expect this list to grow significantly in 2026. The U.S. made big strides toward crypto regulatory clarity in 2025, including passing the GENIUS Act (on stablecoins), rescinding SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 (on custody), introducing Generic Listing Standards for crypto ETPs, and addressing traditional banking access for the crypto industry (Exhibit 9). Next year we expect another major step forward with the passing of bipartisan market structure legislation. The House passed its version of this legislation in July — known as the Clarity Act — and the Senate has since taken up its own process. While there are many details to be ironed out, broadly speaking the legislation provides a traditional finance rulebook for crypto capital markets, including registration and disclosure requirements, classifications of crypto assets, and rules for insiders. In practice, a more complete regulatory framework for crypto assets across the U.S. and other major economies could mean that regulated financial services firms report digital assets on balance sheet and begin transacting on the blockchain. It may also allow for on-chain capital formation, with both startups and mature firms issuing regulated tokens. By further unlocking the full potential of blockchain technology, regulatory clarity should help lift the crypto asset class in general. Because of the potential importance of regulatory clarity in driving the crypto asset class in 2026, a breakdown of bipartisan process in legislation in Congress should be considered a downside risk, in our view. 2025: outstanding supply reached $300 billion and monthly transactions averaged $1.1 trillion per month over the six months ending in November[5], the U.S. Congress passed the GENIUS Act, and a wave of institutional capital poured into the industry (Exhibit 10). In 2026 we expect to see the practical results: stablecoins integrated into cross-border payments services, stablecoins as collateral on derivatives exchanges, stablecoins on corporate balance sheets, and stablecoins as an alternative to credit cards in online consumer payments. Continued growth in the popularity of prediction markets may also drive new demand for stablecoins. Higher stablecoin volumes should benefit the blockchains that record these transactions (e.g., ETH, TRX, BNB, and SOL, U.S. policymakers made two changes related to staking in 2025 that should allow more token holders to participate in this activity: (i) the SEC clarified that liquid staking activities do not constitute securities transactions[9], and (ii) the IRS and Treasury said that investment trusts/ETPs may stake digital assets.[10] The guidance around liquid staking services may benefit Lido and Jito, the leading liquid staking protocols by TVL on Ethereum and Solana, respectively.[11] More broadly, the fact that crypto ETPs are able to stake will likely make this the default structure for holding investment positions in Proof of Stake tokens, resulting in higher stake ratios and pressure on reward rates[12] (Exhibit 17). In an environment where staking is more broadly adopted, custodial staking through ETPs will offer a convenient structure to capture the rewards, while on-chain non-custodial liquid staking will have the advantages of composability within DeFi. We expect this dual structure to persist for some time. We see a bright outlook for digital assets in 2026, underpinned by the dual forces of macro demand for alternative stores of value and improving regulatory clarity. Next year is likely to be about deepening the connectivity between blockchain-based finance and traditional finance, and about institutional capital inflows. The tokens seeing institutional adoption are likely to be those with a clear use case, sustainable revenue, and access to regulated trading venues and applications. Investors can expect to see an expansion of the range of crypto assets available through ETPs, with staking enabled whenever possible. At the same time, regulatory clarity and institutional adoption are likely to raise barriers to entry to mainstream success. For example, crypto projects may be required to meet new registration and disclosure requirements to access regulated exchanges. Institutional investors are also likely to ignore crypto assets without a clear use case — even those with relatively high market caps. The GENIUS Act created a clear distinction between regulated payment stablecoins — which will have certain rights and responsibilities under U.S. law — and other stablecoins — which will not have the same rights. Similarly, we expect crypto’s institutional era to create sharper distinctions between assets with access to regulated venues and institutional capital, and those without the same access. Crypto is entering a new era, and not every token will make a successful transition from the old one.

results.title: US Crypto Policy Tracker Regulatory Developments
highlights: Follow below for the latest regulatory developments related to blockchain, cryptocurrencies, and digital assets from agencies and other regulatory bodies including the SEC, CFTC, FRB, OCC, FDIC, CFPB, Treasury, FinCEN, OFAC, DOJ, DOL, FINRA, and FASB. Last updated September 2026. On August 18, 2026, the SEC proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, establishing tailored offering exemptions, a principles-based disclosure regime, and a conditional safe harbor from the term “investment contract” in the definitions of “security” in the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. If the conditions of the proposed safe harbor are satisfied, then a cryptoasset would not be deemed subject to an investment contract for purposes of those definitions of “security.” On June 2, 2026, the SEC published a Draft Strategic Plan (the Plan) for fiscal years 2026-2030. The Plan designates digital assets and distributed ledger technology as the agency’s first regulatory objective under Goal 1. Objective 1.1 calls for the SEC to “[p]rovide a firm regulatory foundation for digital assets and distributed ledger technologies through a rational, coherent, and principled approach.” The Plan describes blockchain and cryptoasset technologies as having “the potential to revolutionize America’s financial infrastructure” and identifies several concrete priorities: clarifying the boundaries of securities law as applied to digital assets, enabling compliant capital formation through tokenized offerings, supporting development of on-chain financial infrastructure, and ensuring that custody, trading, and staking services can operate “under appropriate oversight without duplicative or conflicting requirements.” The Plan explicitly flags SEC-CFTC jurisdictional coordination, stating that “[t]his harmonization seeks to ensure that the crypto markets have clear and principled rules of the road, anchored in statute, that promotes innovation while maintaining the highest degree of investor protection.” On March 17, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or the Commission), joined by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), issued a comprehensive interpretation (the Interpretive Release) clarifying how federal securities laws apply to cryptoassets and transactions involving cryptoassets. SEC Approves Generic Listing Standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares On September 17, 2025, the SEC approved proposed rule changes by three national securities exchanges to adopt generic listing standards for exchange-traded products (ETPs) that hold spot commodities, including digital assets. Such ETPs will be permitted to list and trade on exchanges without being subject to prior SEC approval under Section 19(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Formerly, exchanges like Nasdaq, NYSE Arca, and Cboe BZX would file a 19b-4 form with the SEC to propose a change to their own rules, allowing them to list a specific crypto exchange-traded fund (ETF). Concurrently, the crypto ETF issuer would file an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for the actual ETF product. Once the SEC acknowledged and published the 19b-4 filing on the Federal Register, a formal clock started for the SEC’s review and potential approval or rejection of the rule change (S-1 filings are not subject to the same deadline-driven process as 19b-4 filings). By establishing generic listing standards, exchanges can now list ETFs without filing for individual rule changes, and issuers only need to file S-1 forms for approval. The SEC has also reportedly requested that issuers withdraw their existing 19b-4 filings. This change is expected to significantly accelerate the launch of new spot crypto ETFs. 2025 SEC Issues Omnibus Approval for Spot Bitcoin Exchange-Traded Products On January 10, 2024, the SEC issued, on an accelerated basis, an Omnibus Approval Order (the Order) for proposed NYSE Arca, Nasdaq, and Cboe BZX rule changes seeking to list and trade shares of 11 spot bitcoin trusts. Spot bitcoin trusts hold actual bitcoin, as opposed to bitcoin futures trusts, which hold derivatives tied to the price of bitcoin. The approval of these rule change requests represents a green light for spot bitcoin-based exchange traded products (ETPs) to trade on national securities exchanges for the first time in bitcoin’s 15-year history, after a decade of attempts by market participants to obtain such approval. In the Order, the SEC found the proposals to be “consistent with the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the Exchange Act) and rules and regulations thereunder applicable to a national securities exchange,” including the requirement that the exchanges’ rules be designed to “prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices.” On May 29, 2026, the CFTC issued four related releases approving and providing initial regulatory guidance for cryptoasset perpetual futures contracts, a product class that has become the dominant form of crypto-derivative trading globally but has until now developed almost entirely on offshore venues due to regulatory uncertainty. The CFTC issued an Order of Approval (the Order) permitting a registered designated contract market (DCM) to list a cash-settled perpetual futures contract referencing the spot price of Bitcoin. The Order permits the requesting DCM to list a cash-settled perpetual contract referencing the spot price of Bitcoin. As described in the Order, the contract references a specific Bitcoin reference price index; has no fixed expiration date and is perpetual in duration; and the contract will trade 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, subject to any trading halts imposed by the DCM. Consistent with perpetual contracts that have emerged offshore, the perpetual contract will employ a periodic funding mechanism whereby long and short position holders exchange funding payments that are based on the difference between the contract’s mark price and the underlying reference price to maintain price convergence with the underlying reference price. Resolving uncertainty that has hindered the emergence of perpetual contracts in the US, the CFTC confirmed in the Order that the Bitcoin perpetual contract in question constitutes a futures contract (i.e., a contract for sale of a commodity for future delivery) for purposes of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) and CFTC rules. In doing so, the CFTC did not object to the requesting DCM’s analysis that a contract without a fixed termination date can still satisfy the “futurity” requirement, relying on the Seventh Circuit precedent of CME v. SEC, holding that futurity “exists where contracts provide for future executory payment obligations, not only where a contract has a final settlement date and fixed term.” The CFTC also emphasized in the Order that perpetual contracts exhibit price convergence in a similar way to traditional futures contracts (albeit via the distinct funding rate mechanism) and that the Bitcoin spot market’s “deep, broadly distributed, active, and continuous trading” supports the effective functioning of this mechanism and “reduc[es] the susceptibility of the contract to manipulation.” The CFTC emphasized that contract categorization must be done on a case-by-case basis, and that the Order’s analysis is expressly limited to the approved contract and similarly structured perpetuals referencing Bitcoin or other digital commodities (as defined in the March 2026 SEC-CFTC joint guidance) with deep, active, and continuous spot market trading, but does not extend to other asset classes. Of note in this regard, and in contrast to the wide use of self-certification for most DCM contract listings, the Order represents the result of a submission for advance CFTC review and approval pursuant to CFTC Rule 40.3 (rather than an ex post review following a self-certification pursuant to CFTC Rule 40.2). 25-38).

highlights: On October 5, 2026, Chairman Michael S. Selig used his remarks at the Fordham Law Blockchain Regulatory Symposium to introduce an advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM) on Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (Regulation CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (Regulation CAM) [1]. The same day, Chairman Selig made the case to a broader audience in a Wall Street Journal op-ed, "CFTC's New Rules for Crypto." He called the ANPRM the CFTC's "first round of regulations for crypto markets" and ended with a line that sums up the agency's position: "The last chapter of crypto regulation was written by crisis. The new frontier of finance will be written by opportunity, innovation and clear rules." The ANPRM rests on section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA). That provision covers retail commodity transactions offered on a leveraged, margined or financed basis. The prior administration used it mainly as an enforcement tool; the Commission now proposes to use it to write "fit-for-purpose" rules. The ANPRM interprets section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act with respect to transactions and markets in crypto assets (as defined in the ANPRM) to "provide notice of its intent to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework comprised of fit-for-purpose rules concerning section 2(c)(2)(D)" with respect to "Crypto Asset Transactions," or the retail commodity transactions described in 2c2d that involve crypto assets. The ANPRM provides a history of the CFTC's regulation of crypto assets and 2c2d transactions in several phases: (i) early commission approach to crypto asset markets (2014-2020), (ii) regulation by enforcement (2021-2024), (iii) President Trump’s working group on Digital Asset Markets (2025) and (iv) regulatory clarity for crypto asset markets. Part (iv) highlights the work of Chairman Selig and the harmonization between the SEC and the CFTC this year. Regulation CTX would interpret key statutory terms, chiefly "offer" and "actual delivery," as they apply to crypto assets and would treat trading on or subject to DCM rules of certain transactions involving crypto assets that are leveraged, margined or financed (or offered on such a basis) as covered transactions under CEA Section 2(c)(2)(D). Regulation CAM would create a new category of designated contract market (DCM), the crypto asset market (CAM), with rules tailored to these transactions – a subcategory of DCM that would be limited to markets that trade only in covered transactions under Reg CTX. The ANPRM states that the Commission preliminarily believes that Reg CAM would permit a DCM to offer crypto asset transactions (CTXs) under its current registration. State Law: The ANPRM states that " The Commission preliminarily believes that in subjecting 2(c)(2)(D) transactions, and thus CTXs, to such comprehensive regulation, Congress made clear that varying state laws did not apply to the operating of trading facilities that offer CTXs” and takes issue with the current state money transmitter licensing and regulations and suggests a strategy similar to that taken in prediction markets cases." Sen. Richard Blumenthal is asking Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald to hand over records on its business relationship with Tether, the issuer of USDT, the world’s largest stablecoin—the dollar-pegged digital asset that underpins the crypto economy. The letter went to Brandon Lutnick, Cantor’s chairman and Howard Lutnick’s son, from Blumenthal as the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. It is a request for information with an Oct. 23 deadline rather than a subpoena, and it describes the minority’s probe as an investigation into “the illicit use of cryptocurrencies and the Trump Administration’s self-enrichment and self-dealings with cryptocurrency firms.” The letter does not accuse Cantor of breaking a specific law, and nothing in it is a finding of wrongdoing. It asks how the firm checks that Tether follows U.S. sanctions and anti-money-laundering rules, and the claims about Tether and the Lutnick family are Blumenthal’s, built on press reports and his staff’s earlier work. “Given the longstanding and deeply intertwined relationship between Tether and Cantor Fitzgerald, and its substantial relationships within the Trump Administration, I am writing to request information about your business partnership with Tether and to learn about your practices for detecting violations of American banking and sanctions laws,” the senator added. Blumenthal wrote that Lutnick has made more than $250 million since President Donald Trump returned to office, including a $192 million distribution from Cantor. Over the same stretch, he said, Cantor’s 5% stake in Tether climbed from $600 million to an estimated $10 billion, on top of the tens of millions of dollars a year the firm collects from the assets it holds for Tether. Howard Lutnick ran Cantor until the Senate confirmed him as Commerce Secretary in February 2025, and the firm is now chaired by his son Brandon. The senator also requests the terms of any loan or legal strategy that would allow Lutnick to transfer asset ownership to his children. The letter landed 10 days after the subcommittee’s Democratic staff released “Tethered to Terrorism,” a report finding that 84% of 846 crypto wallets (addresses that hold tokens) sanctioned or targeted for seizure over links to Iran and its proxies used USDT exclusively or nearly exclusively. Tether, which can lock a wallet so the tokens inside cannot move, published a statement the same day citing roughly $550 million in Iran-linked freezes this year, including $344 million in April and more than $130 million in July. It did not address the report directly. Blumenthal also wants Howard Lutnick’s own records on Tether from his time at Cantor, including “any discussion of Tether with the White House or state and federal regulators, lobbying on Tether’s behalf.” Other requests cover Cantor’s know-your-customer policies (the checks a firm runs on who it does business with), whether it has ever weighed ending the relationship, and its communications with the President’s Council of Advisors on Digital Assets. highlights: On October 5, 2026, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (the “CFTC”) released an Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANPRM”), as approved by the Commission and subject to pre-publication technical corrections, seeking comment on a potential comprehensive, tailored framework for retail commodity transactions involving crypto assets (“CTXs”) under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”). The action comes as the Senate failed to invoke cloture on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025 (the “CLARITY Act”) on September 15, 2026, and as the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) advances its own digital-asset framework through Regulation Crypto Assets and temporary exemptive relief for tokenized securities venues (“TSVs”). Together, the CFTC and SEC actions indicate that, in the near term, agency rulemaking and exemptive action will play an increasingly significant role in shaping the regulatory landscape for digital assets as comprehensive legislation remains uncertain. Legislative Backdrop The House passed the CLARITY Act (H.R. 3633) in July 2025 with bipartisan support, but the Senate failed to invoke cloture on September 15, 2026, by a 49–50 vote, with forty-four (44) Democrats, two (2) Independents and four (4) Republicans voting against it, and one (1) Democrat not voting. The bill would have established a federal digital-asset framework but stalled amid disputes concerning official conflicts of interest, law-enforcement concerns regarding noncustodial developers, and banking group concerns regarding stablecoin yield. With the Senate not scheduled to return to legislative business until November 9 and the 119th Congress nearing its end, the bill is unlikely to see further action and would need to be reintroduced after the new Congress convenes in January 2027. On October 5, 2026, the CFTC began a formal rulemaking process by seeking public comment before drafting rules governing retail crypto asset trading. The ANPRM covers transactions in crypto assets that fall under CEA Section 2(c)(2)(D) and asks how a tailored set of rules for that activity should be designed. Because it is an advanced notice, it frames questions rather than proposing regulatory text, and any binding requirements would need to be adopted through subsequent rulemaking. On September 17, the CFTC submitted Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (“Regulation CTX”) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (“Regulation CAM”) to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review, which concluded on October 2. The October 5 ANPRM then publicly outlined the CFTC’s contemplated framework for Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM, using its existing CEA authorities. The ANPRM states that the Commission’s statutory mandates require it to consider, and solicit comment on, among other matters: (i) clarifying how market participants may elect to conduct business in crypto asset markets under a uniform set of regulations that provides a national regime for CTXs, while preserving access to other markets; (ii) providing crypto asset-specific contextual information regarding requirements and practices that the Commission has found to represent best-practice means of compliance; and (iii) codifying a subcategory of designated contract market registration, known as a crypto asset market, purpose-built for CTXs. The contemplated Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM frameworks are intended to provide a “purpose-fit option for crypto-asset exchanges that wish to operate under a single federal market-regulatory scheme.” Unlike the CLARITY Act, the regulations would not require all crypto asset trading to occur on CFTC-registered platforms. Instead, the CFTC’s on-exchange requirement would apply where retail customers are offered leverage, margin, or financing, including trades the customer chooses to fully pay for, but only until the customer takes actual delivery of the crypto asset (for example, by transfer to a wallet the customer controls). Once actual delivery occurs, the CFTC preliminarily believes the transaction falls outside the on-exchange requirement, subject only to the CFTC’s antifraud and antimanipulation authority. Chairman Selig stated the CFTC lacks authority to impose a mandatory CFTC-platform requirement without congressional action. In August, the SEC proposed rules titled “Regulation Crypto Assets.” The proposal includes two exemptions from Securities Act registration requirements tailored to certain investment contracts involving crypto assets: a one-time “startup” exemption permitting offerings of up to $5 million during a four-year period, and a “fundraising” exemption permitting offerings of up to $75 million during each 12-month period. Under both exemptions, issuers would provide principles-based disclosures and remain subject to the antifraud and antimanipulation provisions of the federal securities laws. Issuers relying on the $75 million fundraising exemption would also be required to provide financial statements and be subject to ongoing reporting requirements. The proposal also includes a conditional safe harbor from the term “investment contract” in the definitions of “security” under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934: if the safe-harbor conditions are satisfied, a crypto asset would no longer be deemed subject to an investment contract. The proposed rules would also preempt state securities law registration and qualification requirements for certain offerings and secondary-market transactions. Public comments are due October 20, 2026. In parallel with the CFTC’s regulatory initiative, the SEC issued an “ Innovation Exemption,” granting temporary, conditional exemptive relief to TSVs from the Exchange Act definition of “exchange,” permitting them to trade tokenized National Market System (“NMS”) stocks using permissioned, innovative automated market makers and liquidity pools. The order also grants a temporary exemption from the Exchange Act definition of “dealer” for certain liquidity providers. Key conditions include symbol and volume limits; same-rights verification for tokenized stock; issuer notice and objection rights; auditable, public smart contracts on public, permissionless distributed ledgers; and coordinated trading halts with the underlying NMS stock. The exemptions are effective for five years, through September 17, 2031. SEC Chairman Paul Atkins linked the action directly to the CLARITY Act’s failure, stating that “Congress was unsuccessful in advancing the CLARITY Act” and that the SEC was taking a statutory-authority step to facilitate onchain trading. The ANPRM begins a formal CFTC rulemaking process to develop a comprehensive, fit-for-purpose framework for retail CTXs and markets under current CFTC authorities. The ANPRM does not itself establish new binding requirements but is intended to solicit market input to inform future The SEC has proposed Regulation Crypto Assets and issued temporary exemptive relief to facilitate onchain trading by TSVs as part of its parallel effort to develop a regulatory framework for crypto assets under the federal securities laws. The Regulation Crypto Assets comment period is still open, and market participants have until October 20, 2026, to submit comments. Because the CFTC and SEC digital asset initiatives are being pursued through agency rulemaking and exemptive action rather than legislation, the resulting regulatory framework is more susceptible to modification by future Commissions than a framework established by Congress. The near-term prospect of digital asset legislation has dimmed with the failure of the CLARITY Act to advance in the Senate. An effort to develop a legislative framework for digital assets will need to begin again after a new Congress convenes in January 2027.

The document carries the reference ESMA75-113276571-1742 and the title "Opinion on the provision of crypto asset services in relation to non-MiCA-compliant asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens". An opinion is a formal statement by ESMA addressed to the national supervisory authorities, through which the authority seeks to establish a consistent supervisory practice across the EU; the legal basis is Article 29(1)(a) of the ESMA Regulation, Regulation (EC) No 1095/2010. The key sentence sits in paragraph 12 and is terse: in ESMA's view, crypto service providers should not provide crypto asset services in relation to ARTs or EMTs that fail to meet the requirements of MiCA. No reprieve, no grandfathering clause, no carve-out for tokens that keep running on a purely technical level. The opinion thereby builds on the earlier line drawn by the European Commission's Q&A 2404 and an older public statement from ESMA, and tightens it noticeably. One point matters for context. In paragraph 7, ESMA says explicitly that it is not changing its existing position and is not claiming that every individual service around such a token automatically amounts to an offer to the public or an admission to trading within the meaning of Articles 16 and 48 of MiCA. Instead it sets out a broader supervisory expectation: whether an authorised provider may continue to offer such services is measured against its obligations under Title V of MiCA. A token is non-MiCA-compliant, according to the footnote in the opinion, where the conditions for a lawful offer to the public or an admission to trading in the EU under Title III or Title IV of MiCA are not met, including any exemptions and transitional provisions. A warning does not prevent the token from remaining available and usable. And a provider's own risk assessment presupposes complex legal and operational judgements that would differ from firm to firm. Clients, as a result, could hardly assess the significance of missing safeguards accurately. Paragraph 21 draws the circle of affected services widely. It covers the operation of a trading platform, exchange services, the execution of orders, the reception and transmission of orders, the placing of crypto assets, advice, transfer services, custody and portfolio management. Under paragraph 22, firms are to put in place technical, contractual and organisational controls that prevent EU clients from building or increasing positions in such tokens. That is an instruction aimed at system architecture, not at the small print. results.title: CFTC Plans Federal License for Leveraged Crypto Exchanges in 2026 | Block Advisor AI
highlights: CFTC Plans Federal License for Leveraged Crypto Exchanges in 2026 | Block Advisor AI October 09, 2026 → Neutral 10 min read CFTC Plans Federal License for Leveraged Crypto Exchanges in 2026 The CFTC's Oct. 5 Regulation CTX and CAM notice would let federally licensed exchanges offer retail crypto margin, while wallet withdrawals stay outside the regime. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission wants to give U.S. crypto exchanges a federal license, and the trigger is leverage. Its Oct. 5 advance notice on Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM sketches a new kind of CFTC-registered venue that could legally offer retail traders margin on spot crypto, a product that today lives almost entirely offshore. For ordinary buyers, the more important detail may be the off-ramp: in the CFTC's preliminary view, crypto you withdraw to a wallet you control falls outside the regime. The CFTC published an advance notice of proposed rulemaking (Release 9307-26, RIN 3038-AF80) seeking comment on two linked frameworks under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act, the Dodd-Frank-era provision that treats leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity deals "as if" they were futures. - Regulation CTX (Crypto Asset Transactions) would interpret when that provision applies to retail crypto trades, which the agency calls CTXs. - Regulation CAM (Crypto Asset Markets) would create a "crypto asset market," a new, narrower subcategory of designated contract market (DCM) built for those trades. An advance notice is the earliest stage of rulemaking. The ANPRM text asks dozens of questions but contains no proposed rule language, and comments are due 60 days after it appears in the Federal Register. As of Oct. 8, it had not yet been published there, according to law firm Fenwick, so the comment clock has not started. The timing is a direct response to Congress. The Senate failed to invoke cloture on the CLARITY Act on Sept. 15, which left the U.S. without a market structure law. In a Wall Street Journal op-ed the CFTC republished, Selig wrote that the agency is proposing rules "following the Senate's failure to advance the Clarity Act this month," and that, unlike that bill, these rules would not force crypto to trade on CFTC platforms. "We don't have the authority to impose such a requirement without congressional action," he wrote. The SEC is running a parallel track. Its proposed Regulation Crypto Assets is open for comment through Oct. 20, and on Oct. 1 it proposed custody rules for advisers and funds, which we covered in our breakdown of the SEC custody proposal. Fenwick's read is that the two agencies are now "building federal crypto market structure through rulemaking rather than legislation." The core idea is simple: the CFTC has no general authority over plain spot crypto trading, but it does have authority over retail trades offered with leverage. Selig described the result as a three-rung ladder in remarks at Fordham Law's Blockchain Regulatory Symposium, as summarized by Fenwick: - Rung 1, spot only: fully paid purchases with no offer of leverage stay with state money transmission regulators, plus CFTC anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority. Nothing changes here. - Rung 2, spot plus leverage: margined, leveraged or financed crypto would have to trade on a CFTC-registered venue, either a new CAM or an existing DCM. - Rung 3, derivatives: perpetuals, futures, options and swaps keep requiring full DCM registration. read most closely is how little it takes to land on Rung 2. The statute covers transactions "offered" with leverage, not just those entered into with it. The ANPRM says that reaches deals Citing the Ninth Circuit's CFTC v. Monex Credit Co. decision, the ANPRM says actual delivery needs "some meaningful degree of possession or control," which for crypto "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." Katten highlights the distinction the notice draws: For tokens with staking or governance rights, the bar may be higher. Fenwick says delivery may require the ability to govern "directly and on a disintermediated basis" and to stake "without being subject to fees charged by an intermediary." Exchange-run cold storage likely does not count if the exchange holds the keys, and the CFTC withdrew its 2020 guidance that had treated delivery to an exchange-affiliated depository as actual delivery, effective Dec. 10, 2025. In his speech, Selig put the intended rule plainly, per Fenwick: delivery to a user's external, non-custodial wallet within 28 days should generally satisfy the exception. The agency's preliminary understanding is that many on-chain trading protocols already settle that way. - FCM intermediation: every CTX on a CAM would run through a futures commission merchant, bringing customer-funds, capital, disclosure and Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering requirements. The CFTC is considering a limited-purpose FCM registration for crypto. What the framework does not do matters as much. CoinDesk's Jesse Hamilton points out that the CFTC still cannot oversee plain spot markets, the unleveraged buying and selling of bitcoin and ether, beyond policing fraud and manipulation. Katten quotes the ANPRM saying CAMs are not meant to "interfere with the legitimate spot market." State money transmitter licenses remain the main rulebook for most retail buying, which is exactly the gap the CLARITY Act was supposed to close. One wrinkle could still pull state-licensed firms toward the federal path. Fenwick notes the CFTC's observation that the Money Transmission Modernization Act, enacted in whole or part by 31 states, excludes DCMs and registered FCMs, so a CAM could shed some state licensing burden. - Customer protection in a failure: current CFTC rules do not let a lender hold a security interest in assets in an FCM's segregated customer account, which sits awkwardly with the leverage model. The agency asks how customer crypto would be treated in an FCM insolvency and floats UCC Article 8 as an alternative to bankruptcy-code protections. - Liens and liquidations: Fenwick calls the notice "internally inconsistent" on whether an outstanding lien defeats actual delivery. The answer decides whether on-chain margin protocols with automatic liquidation are inside or outside the regime. - Securities overlap: the CFTC asks how to handle tokens claimed to be securities and how to treat NFTs, which ties CAM listings to the SEC-CFTC token taxonomy issued earlier this year. Regulatory process rarely moves prices on its own, and nothing in this notice changes what any exchange can offer today. Its effect is on the medium-term map: which U.S. platforms add margin products, how they hold customer coins, and whether self-custody becomes the default line between federal and state oversight. For most buyers, nothing changes yet. Spot purchases on state-licensed exchanges continue as before, and the formal comment period has not even opened. If you are still picking a platform, our best crypto exchange for beginners guide covers the U.S. and EU options on fees, licensing and custody. Three things are worth tracking as this moves. First, watch whether exchanges you use add or remove margin language from their terms, because under the CFTC's reading that single clause can change how your entire account is regulated. Second, the actual-delivery test rewards holding your own keys. Withdrawing to a non-custodial wallet is already the strongest protection against an exchange failure, and the CFTC is now signaling it is also the cleanest line in the rulebook. Third, the comment fight over customer-asset protection in an FCM insolvency will decide whether federally licensed leverage is actually safer than the offshore products it is meant to replace. Until those answers arrive in a proposed rule, treat Regulation CTX and CAM as a direction of travel, not a new set of rights.

What they can still do, through a wind-down window, is let existing holders sell, convert to a compliant stablecoin, withdraw or transfer their balances. National regulators across the bloc have until January 8, 2027 -- three months out -- to see that unwind through. MiCA's stablecoin provisions have technically applied since June 2024, and the regulation's full platform-level rules took effect across the EU on July 1 of this year. USDT's absence from the compliant list isn't new information -- Tether has resisted the reserve-disclosure and e-money-license structure MiCA demands, and has instead leaned on its dominance everywhere outside Europe. What's new is that ESMA has now spelled out, in writing, that platforms tolerating the gap are themselves out of line with the rules, closing off the ambiguity that let some EU exchanges keep USDT pairs live this long. ESMA's own language leaves little room to read around it: "ESMA considers that CASPs should not provide crypto-asset services in relation to ARTs or EMTs that are not compliant with the applicable requirements under MiCA." That's regulator-speak for asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens -- MiCA's two stablecoin categories -- and it's about as direct as EU financial guidance gets. | Detail | Value | | --- | --- | | Guidance issued | Thursday, October 8, 2026 | | Wind-down deadline | January 8, 2027 | | MiCA stablecoin rules in force since | June 2024 | | MiCA full platform rules in force since | July 1, 2026 | | Named non-compliant tokens | USDT (Tether), PYUSD (PayPal USD) | | USDT composite price (Coinaligator, Oct 9) | $1.0004 | | PYUSD composite price (Coinaligator, Oct 9) | $0.9990 | | USDC composite price, for comparison (MiCA-authorized) | $0.9998 | The composite data is the tell: this is a market-access story, not a solvency or confidence story. Nothing about USDT's reserves or redemption mechanics changed this week -- what changed is that EU platforms now have a regulator in writing telling them the token can't stay on offer. That's a very different kind of pressure than a de-peg scare, and it's one Tether has absorbed before by simply not needing the EU as much as the EU might assume. Tether's volume is overwhelmingly non-European -- Latin America, Asia and emerging-market trading desks that never ran through EU-licensed venues in the first place -- so the practical effect lands hardest on EU-based exchanges, which now have to either delist USDT pairs outright or geofence them away from EU customers while serving everyone else normally. PYUSD is the more interesting casualty. Unlike Tether, PayPal has spent the past year explicitly trying to build out EU-compliant stablecoin infrastructure rather than skip the region. Getting named in the same guidance as USDT -- a token whose issuer has shown no urgency about EU licensing -- is a reminder that MiCA's bar doesn't grade on effort. A token is either authorized or it isn't, and PYUSD isn't, at least not yet. January 8 is now a real date on the stablecoin calendar, not a vague compliance horizon. EU exchanges have three months to either get USDT and PYUSD users converted into MiCA-authorized tokens or push those balances out the door entirely, and the rest of the stablecoin market -- Circle's USDC chief among them -- is the obvious beneficiary of whatever liquidity moves as a result. The pegs themselves aren't the story. Who's still allowed to trade them in Europe come January is.

highlights: Chair Michael Selig says only federally registered crypto exchanges can offer leverage under the new framework, closing offshore 100x venues to US traders. The statement sharpened a framework the CFTC opened for public comment on October 5. The agency published an Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking covering two proposed rule sets, Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). Together they would give crypto exchanges the first defined federal path to offer margin and leverage on spot crypto to US retail customers. Selig wrote a companion column in The Wall Street Journal laying out the market structure logic. “Today’s action is a critical step in the CFTC’s ongoing efforts to ensure America remains the crypto capital of the world,” he said in the release. In the WSJ piece he framed the rules as a response to a legislative failure: the Senate could not advance the CLARITY Act on September 15, but President Trump directed agencies to put a crypto market structure in place with or without legislation. , Regulation CTX One important detail: a “covered offer” of terms of service every transaction in CFTC rules, including fully paid If an exchange’s standard terms margin anywhere, it cannot keep alongside a leverage Regulation CAM would create a new subcategory of designated contract market, purpose-built for these crypto transactions. Exchanges registering as a CAM would clear through a derivatives clearing organization and have retail trades intermediated by a futures commission merchant, a structure much closer to a traditional futures exchange than to a modern crypto platform. Leverage itself would only be available through an FCM or an FCM-sponsored bank, with terms laid out in the exchange’s rulebook and per-user financing done through bilateral agreements. Most retail crypto leverage in the world today runs through platforms registered outside the United States. Many of these venues offer 50x to 100x positions. Selig’s framing turns leverage into a licensed activity rather than a product feature. In his telling, high offshore leverage is not a gray area waiting for new rules. It was already outside the law, and the new framework simply names the lane where it can legally exist. The CFTC has used this same provision of the Commodity Exchange Act, Section 2(c)(2)(D), to bring enforcement actions against centralized exchanges and DeFi protocols since 2021. But it never wrote registration categories or listing standards that a crypto exchange could actually follow. “The agency never used this authority to issue purpose-fit rules for these transactions or platforms, only to enforce,” Selig acknowledged in his column. The practical effect is a closing gap. For offshore venues serving US customers, the message is that leverage is not a product it can quietly extend across the border. For US-registered exchanges, registration becomes something that unlocks a product line competitors cannot legally match. Domestically, Bitnomial already launched the first leveraged retail spot crypto product on a CFTC-registered venue, giving the proposed framework a live example to point to. This is a notice of proposed rulemaking, not a final rule. Comments are due within 60 days of Federal Register publication, which has not happened yet. After comments close, the CFTC still has to publish a formal proposed rule and take a second round of comment, a sequence that will run past the November midterms. Nothing is being enforced yet. Selig himself flagged the durability problem. Rules an agency writes can be rewritten more easily than a law Congress has to repeal, and companies can challenge the CFTC’s reading of its own authority in court. Only Congress can mandate that every crypto exchange register with the commission, so the framework is intentionally optional, not mandatory on the whole market. The framework also does not touch spot-only exchanges beyond the anti-fraud and anti-manipulation the CFTC already has. Platforms that make no covered offer of leverage and deliver crypto into actual customer wallets can keep running under state licensing, which is how most American retail spot trading happens today.
