The Senate rejected the motion to invoke cloture on the CLARITY Act on September 15 by a vote of 49 to 50, fourteen months after the bill passed the House by 294 to 134. This was not a simple procedural setback. Cloture requires 60 votes, meaning at least seven Democratic senators would have had to cross party lines, yet no Democrat voted in favor in the final tally. Democratic opposition was not directed at the design of the market-structure rules—the framework assigning digital commodities to the CFTC while retaining SEC jurisdiction over securities-like assets enjoys broad bipartisan support. The real breaking point was how the bill handled conflicts of interest within the executive branch. Financial disclosures from the Trump family show that the family earned approximately $1.4 billion from crypto-related businesses during the first year of his second term. This figure makes any legislation involving the president's crypto assets inevitably appear to involve self-regulation. Senate Republicans revised the text just hours before the vote, attempting to give state attorneys general greater enforcement authority, but federal enforcement authority would still remain with the Department of Justice. Arizona Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego's statement after the vote went straight to the core issue: the bill failed because Republicans refused to make substantive concessions on provisions involving the president himself. His previously proposed countermeasure required the president to divest his crypto holdings during his term, a demand Republicans considered beyond what was politically feasible for the legislation. Notably, the ethics provision does not apply only to the president. The amendment also restricted federal elected officials and their spouses, as well as federal judges, from holding or issuing digital assets. In practice, however, the president's divestment of his assets remained the sole focus obstructing an agreement throughout the negotiations. A compromise at the Senate level had already taken shape on May 1. The compromise text jointly released by Senators Tillis and Alsobrooks stipulated that crypto companies could not pay stablecoin holders interest or yield in a manner that was “economically or functionally equivalent to an interest-bearing bank deposit,” while allowing rewards based on genuine activities such as transactions or the provision of liquidity. , community banks believe the text leaves room for interpretation and is not a completely airtight ban. In a public statement in late August, ICBA Chair and CEO Rebecca Romero Rainey said there was “no room for The September revision added the most specific operational standards for DeFi regulation. The new text established three criteria for identifying a “non-decentralized finance transaction protocol”: the protocol has a controller capable of changing its functions, operations, or consensus rules; transactions are not carried out entirely according to transparent, pre-coded rules; or any entity can restrict, censor, or prohibit users from accessing the service. A protocol meeting any one of these conditions would be required to register with the CFTC based on the functional activity it actually performs—brokerage, trading, execution, clearing, or custody. The legislative intent of this standard is to distinguish genuinely decentralized protocols that operate automatically through smart contracts from platforms that nominally claim to be decentralized but are substantively controlled by specific entities. The revised version also limited the scope of the DeFi provisions to spot or cash transactions in digital commodities, excluding derivatives and securities-related transactions. For DeFi developers, the specific triggers for registration obligations remain subject to interpretive gray areas. If a protocol upgrades its contracts after a vote by governance-token holders, does that constitute “a controller capable of changing the protocol's functions”? If a liquidity pool is paused under certain circumstances, does that qualify as being “capable of restricting users' access to the service”? The answers will depend on subsequent CFTC rulemaking, which itself remains uncertain. The Senate will enter its election-year recess on October 5 and reconvene on November 6. After excluding the recess, only a handful of legislative days remain for consideration before the current Congress ends in early January. Republican Senator Thom Tillis deliberately switched to voting against the motion, preserving the procedural option to refile it in the future. This approach resembles last year's experience with the GENIUS Act—the stablecoin bill likewise suffered a setback at the cloture stage but ultimately passed the Senate several weeks later. Meanwhile, executive agencies have not waited for Congress. On September 17, the SEC granted a five-year “innovation exemption,” allowing eligible platforms to trade tokenized shares of U.S.-listed companies on public blockchains through automated market makers and liquidity pools. The CFTC also submitted its crypto market-structure rule proposal to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review on September 17, just two days after the Senate vote failed. Neither initiative offers the legal certainty that legislation could provide, but both give market participants an operational basis they can rely on under the existing legal framework. The CLARITY Act's setback should not be understood as a retreat in U.S. crypto regulation, but rather as a change in direction. There is sufficient bipartisan consensus on the core framework for market structure; what is obstructing the bill are conflicts of interest within the executive branch and the stability of bank deposits—issues that are not unique to the crypto industry. With the legislative window narrowing to only a few weeks, SEC and CFTC rulemaking and exemption frameworks are filling the legislative vacuum, while the industry's political resources are turning toward shaping the composition of the next Congress. For market participants, short-term regulatory certainty will come more from interpretive guidance issued by executive agencies than from enacted legislation, meaning compliance strategies need to monitor two parallel rule systems at the same time. Democrats demanded that the bill include an ethics-enforcement mechanism independent of the Department of Justice and restrict the president and his family from holding shares in crypto companies while in office. The current compromise proposal prohibits crypto companies from providing stablecoin yield equivalent to bank-deposit interest, while allowing transaction incentives and liquidity rewards. If the stricter ICBA version is ultimately enacted, stablecoins' function as yield-generating instruments would be materially restricted, potentially changing some users' asset-allocation choices. The September revision requires “non-decentralized” protocols with controllability characteristics to register with the CFTC. Registration depends on whether the protocol is controlled by a specific entity, whether it operates according to pre-coded rules, and whether user access can be restricted. The provisions apply only to spot transactions in digital commodities.

highlights: Solana ETFs Post Record $188M Week as Bitwise Takes Lead Seven US spot Solana ETFs drew a record $188 million in one week, with Bitwise's BSOL taking about 68 percent and Friday's $87 million day the best since launch. Sebastian Szczeblewski · Oct 8, 2026 · 4 min read US spot Solana exchange-traded funds took in about $188 million last week, their biggest weekly haul since launching in October 2025, and all seven funds in the group finished on the positive side, according to weekly flow data shared by Solana’s official account and covered by CoinDesk. The record was front-loaded into a single session. The group added roughly $87 million on Friday, September 25, its best day ever, nearly doubling the previous daily record of $33.5 million set in August. Bitwise’s BSOL received about $56 million of that Friday total and Grayscale’s GSOL about $19 million, with the balance spread across the other five funds. Across the full week, BSOL led with roughly $128.5 million, close to 68 percent of the group’s intake. Grayscale followed with $28.1 million, Fidelity’s FSOL added $18 million, and the four remaining funds, run by Morgan Stanley, VanEck, Franklin Templeton and 21Shares, shared about $14 million between them. The concentration is the more telling number. BSOL has collected roughly $1.22 billion of the $1.6 billion in cumulative net inflows the group has drawn since the funds began trading on October 28, 2025, a share near 76 percent. No other issuer holds anything close to that position in comparable crypto ETF groups, and it continues to make Bitwise the price-setter for how institutional Solana exposure gets packaged in the US market. The record week did not carry over cleanly into October. Weekly figures from SoSoValue, cited by 24/7 Wall St., show the group took in just $2.4 million for the week ending October 2, a drop of about 99 percent from the record week before it. Two sessions in that stretch actually finished in outflows, with $11.1 million leaving on September 30 and $5.9 million on October 1. A $1.3 million inflow on the final day was all that kept the week positive. Net assets at the end of that week stood at about $1.9 billion, down from a record $1.96 billion the week before. Since the funds still took in money, most of the decline came from Solana’s price, not redemptions. Cumulative net inflows now stand at about $1.61 billion, a figure that only moves when cash actually crosses the line, unlike net asset value. Longer-term demand still looks firm. The funds have pulled in roughly $842 million in 2026 so far, including $480 million in the third quarter and $272 million in September alone. The streak of weekly inflows has held without interruption since late June, but the margin has grown thin, and the week running October 5 through 9 will show whether buyers return in size or the streak breaks. The staking structure is doing much of the work. Spot Solana funds hold the token directly and capture staking yield on their holdings, then pass part of that return to shareholders. Bitcoin spot ETFs offer no comparable yield, and issuers have leaned on that difference as a selling point since launch, along with lower asset volatility relative to smaller altcoins. Sheer size also matters. Solana counts 587.9 million tokens in circulation against a market cap near $70 billion at recent prices, so the group’s $1.9 billion in ETF net assets still represents a small slice of the float, leaving room for inflows to move the price if buying accelerates. Bitcoin and ether ETFs, by contrast, hold shares of scarcity that dwarf any plausible monthly flow. Keep an eye on two things as the category matures. First, the concentration: Bitwise’s near-76 percent cumulative share means category-wide totals mostly track one fund’s order flow, which makes the group’s headline numbers look better or worse than the competition underneath. Second, fees and staking terms: if Grayscale, Fidelity or the others cut costs or adjust their yield arrangements, the concentration could erode quickly, since the products hold near-identical assets and differ mainly on cost and payout structure. The flows landed against a soft tape for digital assets. Bitcoin slipped below $83,000 this week as US spot bitcoin ETFs posted their biggest daily outflow since June at $487 million, and ether ETFs are in their sixth straight day of withdrawals with about $160 million leaving on October 7. Rising Treasury yields and oil above $100 have pushed traders to de-risk across the board, and prediction markets now price another Federal Reserve hike as more likely than not. Against that backdrop, the September record in Solana products stands out, though the October fade suggests it reflected positioning rather than a durable change in demand. Nor did the issuers imply the streak was guaranteed: the simplest read of the last two weeks is that Solana ETF demand runs hot and cold, a record burst of buying followed by near-neutral flows, with cumulative totals still climbing because redemptions stay small. One structural note worth holding onto. The funds began trading on October 28, 2025, extending regulated, exchange-listed crypto exposure beyond bitcoin and ether to a third major asset. Some of the early demand came from advisors and funds filling allocations they could not access a year earlier, which is a one-time effect. Whether the category keeps compounding depends on fresh money, and the last two weeks show exactly how much that swings week to week.

This index comprises ten carefully chosen cryptocurrencies: BNB (CRYPTO: BNB), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), Hyperliquid (CRYPTO: HYPE), Chainlink (CRYPTO: LINK), Stellar (CRYPTO: XLM), Sui (CRYPTO: SUI), Uniswap (CRYPTO: UNI), Avalanche (CRYPTO: AVAX), and Aave (CRYPTO: AAVE). CF Benchmarks manages both indexes, publishing updated values every second and daily settlement prices at 4 p.m. in London, New York, and Singapore. However, CME has not launched any futures contracts linked to either index, so these benchmarks currently have no financial tracking. The CME Emerging Crypto Index calculates each coin’s weight based on its free-float market capitalization. This means it considers only coins available for trading and excludes those held back by teams or organizations. results.title: Dogecoin, Litecoin and HBAR ETFs Took In Less Than $10 Million Combined This Week. Do Altcoin Actually Move Prices? - 24/7 Wall St.
highlights: Chainlink ETFs quietly pulled in more money than Solana and XRP funds combined this week, yet the coin's price dropped anyway. The relationship between altcoin ETF flows and actual price moves turns out to be far stranger than most investors… By Sam Daodu Published October 4, 2026, 7:11am ET · 3 min read The ETF Examiner desk. Editor: Ryne Mauck. - Dogecoin, Litecoin, and HBAR ETFs combined pulled in under $10 million last week, too small to move prices against $854 million in daily Dogecoin trading. - Chainlink led all small altcoin ETFs with $8.3 million in weekly inflows, yet its price still fell roughly 2%. - Polkadot funds hold four times what investors deposited, proving price gains drive altcoin ETF size far more than fresh capital. Funds associated with Dogecoin (CRYPTO:DOGE), Litecoin (CRYPTO:LTC), and Hedera’s HBAR (CRYPTO:HBAR) collectively brought in under $10 million during the week from September 28 to October 2, 2026, according to data from SoSoValue. Notably, Dogecoin funds attracted around $879,000 on September 29 but lost about $551,000 the following day. In contrast, Polkadot (CRYPTO:DOT) funds recorded no new investments all week, while Chainlink (CRYPTO:LINK) funds saw a steady stream of inflows. With such low activity in small altcoin ETFs, one might wonder if they can actually influence the prices of the coins they represent. Chainlink Funds Took In $8.3 Million, More Than Solana and XRP Funds Combined This past week, Chainlink saw inflows of about $8.3 million, surpassing the combined inflows of Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) and XRP (CRYPTO:XRP). Chainlink funds saw daily inflows of $2.4 million on September 28, $1.8 million on September 29, $1.4 million on September 30, and $2.6 million on October 1, before leveling off on October 2. This total outpaced Solana’s $2.4 million and XRP’s $4.7 million, which together reached only $7.2 million—suggesting a quiet week in the crypto ETF space. Chainlink’s funds are also the largest among the smaller coins, with about $230 million in assets, or about 2% of Chainlink’s total market value of $10.5 billion. This size advantage might lead to more regular orders through advisory platforms, highlighting the interaction between a fund’s size and its demand. Price changes have a more significant impact on these funds than the actual inflows of new capital. For instance, Polkadot’s funds hold about $11 million yet have seen only $2.6 million invested, about a quarter of their current worth. Similarly, Avalanche (CRYPTO:AVAX) funds hold $57 million against $29 million ever invested, despite minor inflows of about $268,000 during the week. Conversely, Litecoin and HBAR show a different trend. Litecoin’s funds hold about $14.7 million, which is slightly less than the $15.8 million invested, while HBAR funds hold $80 million against $114 million, about 30% less than investors put in. Taking a closer look at price changes during the same week supports this observation. HBAR rose roughly 7% despite only two days of inflows, while Chainlink, whose funds had the strongest inflows, fell about 2%. Meanwhile, Dogecoin dropped about 5%, even though its funds ended the week nearly flat. Daily trading volumes also far exceed the money flowing into these funds. For instance, on October 3, about $854 million of Dogecoin traded, dwarfing the week’s total inflows. At their current levels, small altcoin ETFs do not have a substantial impact on prices. Daily inflows ranging from a few hundred thousand to $2.6 million, arriving over only a few days, are too minimal and inconsistent to affect coins traded around the clock. Take Polkadot as a clear example; its funds hold four times as much as what investors have actually put in, which indicates that price changes have driven these funds up, not the inflows. Liu shared his thoughts on Schwab’s On Investing podcast released on October 2. He observed that retail trading activity in stocks and crypto has moved in the opposite direction from event-contract platforms. These platforms allow traders to buy contracts tied to outcomes like Federal Reserve rate decisions. “You are seeing a share shift happening,” Liu remarked, suggesting that as retail cash moves into one market, it corresponds to a decline in another. The numbers support Liu’s observations. In the year to October 4, Bitcoin fell about 30%, Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) by about 40%, and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) around 47%. By comparison, XRP fell about 50%, and Dogecoin dropped about 63%. Bitcoin has strong institutional backing, with U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs holding about 1.29 million BTC, which may explain its less severe decline. highlights: XRP Ledger Switches On Delegated Permissions, and Solana's Final Cut to 200ms Blocks Goes Live Two Blockchain Upgrades: XRP Ledger Delegation and Solana’s 200ms Blocks Go Live October 9, 2026 Blockchains change through upgrades that their operators switch on at set points. Two this week matter for businesses and app builders. The XRP Ledger has turned on a feature that lets one account give limited powers to another. Solana’s blocks now arrive faster, every 200 milliseconds instead of 250, after a change took effect on Friday afternoon UK time. TSN offers no investment advice. Confirmed on-chain. On the XRP Ledger, changes arrive as “amendments”, which switch on once enough validators (the servers that confirm transactions) support them for two weeks. On Friday morning TSN asked a public XRP Ledger server about the amendment PermissionDelegationV1_1, and it reported it as `"enabled":true` [1]. CoinDesk, citing an amendment tracker, reports that it activated on 8 October (reported) [3]. The official description is short: it “Allows accounts to delegate some permissions to other accounts” [2]. It “replaces PermissionDelegation, fixing a critical bug discovered in the original implementation” [2]. According to CoinDesk, each helper account “can receive up to 10 permissions”, and these limit the kinds of action it can take “rather than automatically imposing a spending cap” [3]. Why it matters. A stablecoin issuer, fund or bank can keep the keys that control its main holdings offline, while separate accounts with narrow powers handle routine jobs such as approving customers or making payments. CoinDesk compares this to how banks already split payment and compliance duties among staff [3]. One caveat. XRPL.org warns: “Until the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment is enabled, it is recommended not to delegate the PaymentBurn granular permission”. Before that fix, a delegate with that permission “can also mint new fungible tokens” in certain circumstances; other permissions are unaffected [2]. CoinDesk reports that the fix “had 27 of 35 validator votes on Friday. It needs 29 to start the two-week countdown that would lift the warning” [3]. Solana: the last step to 200ms blocks is now live Confirmed on-chain: live since about 15:40 BST on Friday. Solana has been cutting its target “slot” time, the interval in which a block can be produced, in steps from 400 milliseconds. The Solana Foundation now says: “Solana’s slot time is now 200ms, down from 400ms. All four staged reductions are active on mainnet; the final step took effect at the start of epoch 1053 on October 9, 2026” [4]. The Foundation dates the earlier steps to 21 August, 28 August and 18 September [4]. The change was designed by Anza, a Solana software developer, in the technical proposal SIMD-0525 [6]. Under that proposal, each step is a “feature gate” that takes effect one epoch (a fixed run of 432,000 slots) after it is switched on [6]. The 200ms switch was flipped at the start of epoch 1052, so it took effect when epoch 1053 began, at slot 454,896,000 [7]. The public network records that slot at 15:40 BST on Friday 9 October, a little earlier than the roughly 16:00 BST that CoinDesk, citing Anza, had expected [5][7]. Anza, Solana’s lead software developer, said minutes later: “200ms slots are now live on mainnet-beta” [13]. TSN’s measurement of the network after the switch showed slots averaging about 215 milliseconds, against about 270 before it [7]. What changes. Blocks now arrive more often, but each carries less. Per SIMD-0525, maximum compute per block falls from 37,500,000 to 30,000,000 units [6], which CoinDesk describes as keeping theoretical capacity “roughly unchanged” [5]. The Solana Foundation also notes that a transaction’s recent-blockhash window, its time limit before it expires, is now “30 seconds”. That gives less slack to offline or manual signing flows, where a person approves a transaction by hand [4]. - That XRPL delegation is risk-free. The PaymentBurn warning stands until a separate fix is enabled [2]. - That Solana’s next big change has arrived. The 200ms slots are live, but Anza says Alpenglow, a separate overhaul of how the network confirms blocks, “is not live on mainnet-beta yet” [4][13]. - That faster blocks mean more total capacity. Per-block limits shrink to match [6]. - That Sei’s FlatKV storage migration is finished, or even under way. Proposal #126 passed and switched it on, but when TSN checked at 18:20 BST Sei had not confirmed that nodes had started migrating, or given a timetable [9][11]. The Bottom Line The XRP Ledger now lets accounts delegate limited powers, so key holdings can stay offline, with one known caveat on token burning. Solana’s final cut to 200ms blocks took effect on Friday afternoon UK time; it brings quicker confirmations, not more capacity, and shorter expiry windows for slow signers. Sei’s mandatory v6.7 upgrade is done, removing IBC and some older interfaces. Its bigger storage change was approved in a separate vote that closed at 17:51 BST on Friday; Sei has yet to confirm when the migration itself is complete.
